questions.question: The patient presented with several mucocutaneous findings. Which specific clinical features are most characteristic of Behçet’s disease (BD) and were present in this case?

In the context of acute neuro-Behçet's disease (neuro-BD), what is the hypothesized pathophysiological mechanism linking CNS inflammation to the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)?
The patient exhibited persistent hiccups and elevated creatine kinase (CK) levels. What clinical condition do these specific findings suggest in the setting of profound hyponatraemia?

When evaluating a patient with fever, headache, and lymphocytic pleocytosis in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), what is the systematic approach to excluding infectious versus non-infectious etiologies of aseptic meningitis?
What are the primary diagnostic criteria for SIADH, and how were they confirmed in this patient’s laboratory results?

While corticosteroids are typically the mainstay of treatment for acute neuro-BD, this patient responded to colchicine monotherapy. What is the pharmacological mechanism of colchicine that may explain its efficacy in suppressing the inflammatory response in this case?
What is the recommended initial management for SIADH, and what is the most critical precaution to take when correcting hyponatraemia in these patients?
Does a normal brain MRI during the acute phase of neurological symptoms rule out a diagnosis of neuro-Behçet’s disease? Explain why.
